es.summary: Conjunto de anomalías congénitas causadas por consumo de alcohol materno durante el embarazo, que incluye defectos cardíacos estructurales.
key_points: El alcohol atraviesa la placenta y afecta el desarrollo cardiaco fetal.
Los defectos cardíacos más comunes son septales y de la gran arteria.
El diagnóstico se basa en criterios clínicos y ecocardiografía.
El manejo incluye vigilancia cardiológica y apoyo multidisciplinario.

pathophysiology: El etanol materno atraviesa la placenta y altera la señalización celular del corazón en desarrollo.
Interfiere con la migración de células del mesodermo y la formación de tabiques cardíacos.
Produce apoptosis y daño oxidativo, resultando en defectos estructurales.
risk_factors: Consumo de alcohol en cualquier trimestre del embarazo.
Binge drinking (≥4‑5 bebidas en una ocasión).
Historia de consumo crónico antes del embarazo.
signs_symptoms: Soplo cardíaco detectable al examen físico.
Cianosis o dificultad respiratoria en recién nacido.
Hipertensión pulmonar secundaria a defectos estructurales.
diagnostics: Ecocardiografía fetal o neonatal: identifica defectos septales, conductuales o de la gran arteria.
Radiografía de tórax: cardiomegalia o congestión pulmonar.
Panel metabólico: descartar otras causas de cardiomiopatía.
treatment: Cirugía cardíaca correctiva según tipo de defecto.
Medicamentos antiarrítmicos o diuréticos (p. ej., furosemida) si hay insuficiencia cardíaca.
Seguimiento con cardiología pediátrica y ecocardiogramas periódicos.
nursing_care: Monitorizar signos vitales, especialmente presión arterial y frecuencia cardíaca.
Evaluar saturación de oxígeno y presencia de soplos en cada turno.
Mantener posición semi‑Fowler para facilitar la expansión pulmonar.
Registrar balance hídrico y observar edema periférico.
patient_teaching: Informar a la familia sobre la importancia del seguimiento cardiológico regular.
Enseñar signos de alarma: dificultad respiratoria, cianosis, aumento de la irritabilidad.
Promover lactancia materna o alimentación adecuada para favorecer el crecimiento.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de disminución de la perfusión tisular cardíaca
outcomes: Perfusión tisular cardíaca: presión arterial sistólica mantenida entre 90‑110 mmHg en 24 h.
Oxigenación: saturación de pulso ≥ 95 % en reposo.

interventions.action: Monitorear presión arterial y frecuencia cardíaca cada 4 h.
interventions.rationale: Detectar precozmente signos de hipoperfusión.

interventions.action: Evaluar y registrar signos de insuficiencia cardíaca (edema, dificultad respiratoria).
interventions.rationale: Permite intervención temprana para evitar deterioro.

interventions.action: Mantener hidratación adecuada según balance hídrico y orden médica.
interventions.rationale: Previene hipovolemia que empeora la perfusión.

interventions.action: Colaborar con el equipo de cardiología para programar ecocardiogramas de control.
interventions.rationale: Facilita la detección de cambios estructurales que afecten el gasto cardíaco.

interventions.action: Educar a los padres sobre signos de alarma y cuándo buscar atención de urgencia.
interventions.rationale: Promueve la detección temprana de deterioro clínico en el hogar.

outcomes: Volumen intravascular: peso estable (+/- 0.5 kg) en 48 h.

interventions.action: Administrar fluidos IV según prescripción y monitorizar balance hídrico.
interventions.rationale: Restablecer el volumen circulante y prevenir hipovolemia.

interventions.action: Evaluar mucosa oral y turgor cutáneo cada 2 h.
interventions.rationale: Detectar signos tempranos de deshidratación.

interventions.action: Registrar ingesta y eliminación de líquidos con precisión.
interventions.rationale: Facilita ajustes de terapia de fluidos.

interventions.action: Asegurar acceso venoso periférico de calibre adecuado.
interventions.rationale: Garantiza la administración segura de fluidos.

interventions.action: Enseñar a los padres la importancia de la alimentación frecuente y adecuada.
interventions.rationale: Previene la pérdida de volumen en el periodo post‑natal.

en.summary: A set of congenital anomalies caused by maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy, including structural heart defects.
key_points: Alcohol crosses the placenta and affects fetal cardiac development.
The most common heart defects are septal and great artery defects.
Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria and echocardiography.
Management includes cardiac surveillance and multidisciplinary support.

pathophysiology: Maternal ethanol crosses the placenta and disrupts cellular signaling in the developing heart.
It interferes with mesodermal cell migration and cardiac septum formation.
It induces apoptosis and oxidative damage, resulting in structural defects.
risk_factors: Alcohol consumption at any trimester of pregnancy.
Binge drinking (≥4‑5 drinks in one occasion).
History of chronic use before pregnancy.
signs_symptoms: Heart murmur detectable on physical exam.
Cyanosis or respiratory distress in the newborn.
Pulmonary hypertension secondary to structural defects.
diagnostics: Fetal or neonatal echocardiography: identifies septal, conduction, or great artery defects.
Chest X‑ray: cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion.
Metabolic panel: rule out other causes of cardiomyopathy.
treatment: Corrective cardiac surgery based on defect type.
Antiarrhythmic or diuretic medications (e.g., furosemide) if heart failure is present.
Follow‑up with pediatric cardiology and periodic echocardiograms.
nursing_care: Monitor vital signs, especially blood pressure and heart rate.
Assess oxygen saturation and presence of murmurs each shift.
Maintain semi‑Fowler position to facilitate lung expansion.
Record fluid balance and monitor for peripheral edema.
patient_teaching: Inform the family about the importance of regular cardiac follow‑up.
Teach warning signs: respiratory distress, cyanosis, increased irritability.
Encourage breastfeeding or appropriate feeding to support growth.

care_plans.diagnosis: Risk for decreased cardiac tissue perfusion
outcomes: Cardiac tissue perfusion: systolic blood pressure maintained between 90‑110 mmHg in 24 h.

interventions.action: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate every 4 h.
interventions.rationale: Detect early signs of hypoperfusion.

interventions.action: Assess and document signs of heart failure (edema, respiratory distress).
interventions.rationale: Allows early intervention to prevent deterioration.

interventions.action: Maintain adequate hydration per fluid balance and medical orders.
interventions.rationale: Prevents hypovolemia that worsens perfusion.

interventions.action: Collaborate with cardiology team to schedule follow‑up echocardiograms.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates detection of structural changes affecting cardiac output.

interventions.action: Educate parents on warning signs and when to seek urgent care.
interventions.rationale: Promotes early detection of clinical decline at home.

outcomes: Intravascular volume: weight stable (+/- 0.5 kg) in 48 h.

interventions.action: Administer IV fluids per prescription and monitor fluid balance.
interventions.rationale: Restore circulating volume and prevent hypovolemia.

interventions.action: Assess oral mucosa and skin turgor every 2 h.
interventions.rationale: Detect early signs of dehydration.

interventions.action: Record intake and output accurately.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates fluid therapy adjustments.

interventions.action: Ensure peripheral venous access of adequate caliber.
interventions.rationale: Guarantees safe fluid administration.

interventions.action: Teach parents the importance of frequent and adequate feeding.
interventions.rationale: Prevents volume loss in the post‑natal period.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: Alcohol can harm your baby at any stage during a pregnancy.

sections.complications.0.quote: Adverse Effects and Contraindications Diltiazem can cause asystole; atrial flutter; first-, second-, and third-degree atrioventricular block; bradycardia; chest pain; congestive heart failure; sinus pause; sinus node dysfunction; syncope; ventricular dysrhythmia; ventricular fibrillation; ventricular tachycardia; dizziness; allergic reaction; Stevens–Johnson syndrome; and angioedema.

sections.complications.2.quote: The problems could include : Abnormal facial features, such as a smooth ridge between the nose and upper lip Small head size Shorter-than-average height Low body weight Poor coordination Hyperactive behavior Difficulty with attention and memory Learning disabilities and difficulty in school Speech and language delays Intellectual disability or low IQ Poor reasoning and judgment skills Sleep and sucking problems as a baby Vision or hearing problem

sections.nursing_care.0.quote: Monitor vital signs frequently, particularly blood pressure, because nitroglycerin can cause significant hypotension.
